Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Workplace safety in hazardous environments like construction sites and industrial plants is crucial to prevent accidents and injuries. One of the most important safety measures is ensuring workers wear safety helmets, which protect against head injuries from falling objects and machinery. Non-compliance with helmet regulations increases the risk of serious injuries or fatalities, making effective monitoring essential, especially in large-scale operations where manual oversight is prone to errors and inefficiency.

To overcome these challenges, SafeGuard Corp plans to develop an automated image analysis system capable of detecting whether workers are wearing safety helmets. This system will improve safety enforcement, ensuring compliance and reducing the risk of head injuries. By automating helmet monitoring, SafeGuard aims to enhance efficiency, scalability, and accuracy, ultimately fostering a safer work environment while minimizing human error in safety oversight.

Objective¶

As a data scientist at SafeGuard Corp, you are tasked with developing an image classification model that classifies images into one of two categories:

  • With Helmet: Workers wearing safety helmets.
  • Without Helmet: Workers not wearing safety helmets.

Data Description¶

The dataset consists of 631 images, equally divided into two categories:

  • With Helmet: 311 images showing workers wearing helmets.
  • Without Helmet: 320 images showing workers not wearing helmets.

Dataset Characteristics:

  • Variations in Conditions: Images include diverse environments such as construction sites, factories, and industrial settings, with variations in lighting, angles, and worker postures to simulate real-world conditions.
  • Worker Activities: Workers are depicted in different actions such as standing, using tools, or moving, ensuring robust model learning for various scenarios.

Plot random images from each of the classes and print their corresponding labels.¶

In [5]:
def plot_images_random(images,labels):
  num_classes = 2 #two classes are 'with helmet' and 'without helmet'
  categories=np.unique(labels['Label']) #finds all unique labels in my arry. Without helmet = 0, With helmet = 1

  # Define the mapping from numerical label to descriptive class name
  label_name_map = {0: 'Without Helmet', 1: 'With Helmet'}

  rows = 2 # two rows because two classes
  cols = 5 #this can be whatever
  fig_size = plt.figure(figsize=(10,8)) #width and height of my fig size image, 10 width, 8 height
  for i in range (cols):
    for j in range(rows):
      random_image = np.random.randint(0,len(labels)) # Get a random index

      # Get the actual label value (0 or 1) for the random image
      actual_label_value = labels.iloc[random_image]['Label'] #iloc = integer-location

      # Get the descriptive name using the map
      descriptive_label = label_name_map[actual_label_value]#turns 0, 1 to With or Without helmet

      ax = fig_size.add_subplot(rows,cols, i * rows + j + 1) #ax short for axes
      ax.imshow(images[random_image,:])
      ax.set_title(descriptive_label) # Use the descriptive label in the title
      ax.axis('off') # Turn off axis to make plot cleaner
  plt.tight_layout() # Adjust layout to prevent titles from overlapping
  plt.show()

Data Preprocessing¶

Converting images to grayscale¶

In [7]:
def convert_to_gray(images):
  #Images_proj is a numpy array, so we create these values to store them
  num_images = images.shape[0]
  height = images.shape[1]
  width = images.shape[2]

  # Create an empty array to store grayscale images
  # Grayscale images have shape (height, width). making sure datatype is the same as images.
  grayscale_images = np.empty((num_images, height, width), dtype=images.dtype)

  for idx in range(num_images):
    grayscale_images[idx] = cv2.cvtColor(images[idx], cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

  return grayscale_images

images_gray = convert_to_gray(images_proj)

To verify that images_gray is truly grayscale, we can check its shape and the data type and range of its pixel values. Grayscale images should have 2 dimensions (height, width) for a single image, or 3 dimensions (number_of_images, height, width) for a collection. The dtype will typically be uint8 for 0-255 pixel values.

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Utility Functions¶

In [12]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using statsmodels
def model_performance_classification(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # Check if the input needs a channel dimension added (e.g., for grayscale images with 3 dims)
    if predictors.ndim == 3: # If shape is (num_images, height, width)
        predictors_processed = np.expand_dims(predictors, axis=-1) # Make it (num_images, height, width, 1)
    else: # Already 4D (num_images, height, width, channels) or another compatible shape
        predictors_processed = predictors

    # checking which probabilities are greater than threshold
    pred = model.predict(predictors_processed).reshape(-1)>0.5

    target = target.to_numpy().reshape(-1)


    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred, average='weighted')  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred, average='weighted')  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred, average='weighted')  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame({"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1 Score": f1,},index=[0],)

    return df_perf
In [13]:
def plot_confusion_matrix(model,predictors,target):
    """
    Function to plot the confusion matrix

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # Check if the input needs a channel dimension added (e.g., for grayscale images with 3 dims)
    if predictors.ndim == 3: # If shape is (num_images, height, width)
        predictors_processed = np.expand_dims(predictors, axis=-1) # Make it (num_images, height, width, 1)
    else: # Already 4D (num_images, height, width, channels) or another compatible shape
        predictors_processed = predictors

    # checking which probabilities are greater than threshold
    pred = model.predict(predictors_processed).reshape(-1)>0.5

    target = target.to_numpy().reshape(-1)

    # Plotting the Confusion Matrix using confusion matrix() function which is also predefined tensorflow module
    confusion_matrix = tf.math.confusion_matrix(target,pred)
    f, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
    sns.heatmap(
        confusion_matrix,
        annot=True,
        linewidths=.4,
        fmt="d",
        square=True,
        ax=ax
    )
    plt.show()

Model 1: Simple Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)¶

In [14]:
#A simple CNN starts with sequential, for simple problems we only need 3-5 layers.
#beginning layers detect simple things. Further in, you want more filters.
#filters should be in powers of two due to success of CNN's with this exponent.
#Conv2D = feature detection Conv2D output = feature maps.
#pooling = summarizer, reduces dimensions, makes NN less reactive to shifts, etc. Reduces compute.
model_1 = Sequential()

# First Convolutional Block
model_1.add(Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation='relu', input_shape=(200, 200, 1))) # 32 filters, 3x3 kernel, ReLU activation
model_1.add(MaxPooling2D((2, 2))) # 2x2 pooling window

# Second Convolutional Block
#second block takes already learned features, and learns more abstract features to combine them
# second maxpooling takes the feature map and makes an even smaller output.

model_1.add(Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu')) # 64 filters, 3x3 kernel, ReLU activation
model_1.add(MaxPooling2D((2, 2)))

# Third Convolutional Block
#each block builds on top of each other to produce a clearer, less affected feature map.
model_1.add(Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation='relu')) # 128 filters, 3x3 kernel, ReLU activation
model_1.add(MaxPooling2D((2, 2)))

# Flatten the output before feeding to Dense layers
#flattens from 3D to 1D.
#dense layers have to be 1D
model_1.add(Flatten())

# Fully Connected Layers (Dense)
#weighted sum, adds bias and sends to activation layer
#weighted sum = all inputs multiplied by a weight, then the sum of the weighted inputs.

model_1.add(Dense(128, activation='relu')) # 128 neurons, ReLU activation
model_1.add(Dropout(0.5)) # Dropout for regularization to prevent overfitting

#1 neuron for binary classifcation, if this was multiple classifications it would be 1 neuron per classification + softmax
model_1.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')) # Output layer with 1 neuron and sigmoid for binary classification

# Compile the model
#if multiple classes, use categorical_crossentropy

model_1.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

# Display model summary
model_1.summary()

Vizualizing the predictions¶

In [16]:
def plot_random_predictions(model, images, true_labels, num_samples=5):
    # Ensure images are in the correct format for prediction (add channel dim)
    if images.ndim == 3:
        images = np.expand_dims(images, axis=-1) # Add a channel dimension for grayscale

    # Get predictions
    predictions = model.predict(images)

    # Select random samples
    indices = np.random.choice(len(images), num_samples, replace=False)

    plt.figure(figsize=(15, 5))
    for i, idx in enumerate(indices):
        plt.subplot(1, num_samples, i + 1)

        # Get original image (remove channel dim for display if added)
        display_image = images[idx].squeeze() # .squeeze() removes single-dimensional entries

        plt.imshow(display_image, cmap='gray')

        true_label_val = true_labels.iloc[idx]['Label']
        predicted_prob = predictions[idx][0]
        predicted_label = 1 if predicted_prob > 0.5 else 0

        true_label_name = 'With Helmet' if true_label_val == 1 else 'Without Helmet'
        predicted_label_name = 'With Helmet' if predicted_label == 1 else 'Without Helmet'

        color = 'green' if true_label_val == predicted_label else 'red'

        plt.title(f"True: {true_label_name}\nPred: {predicted_label_name} ({predicted_prob:.2f})", color=color)
        plt.axis('off')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

print('Training Predictions:')
plot_random_predictions(model_1, X_train_normalized, y_train, num_samples=5)

print('Validation Predictions:')
plot_random_predictions(model_1, X_val_normalized, y_val, num_samples=5)

Model 4: (VGG-16 (Base + FFNN + Data Augmentation)¶

Train Model 4 with Data Augmentation¶

  • In most of the real-world case studies, it is challenging to acquire a large number of images and then train CNNs.

  • To overcome this problem, one approach we might consider is Data Augmentation.

  • CNNs have the property of translational invariance, which means they can recognise an object even if its appearance shifts translationally in some way. - Taking this attribute into account, we can augment the images using the techniques listed below

    • Horizontal Flip (should be set to True/False)
    • Vertical Flip (should be set to True/False)
    • Height Shift (should be between 0 and 1)
    • Width Shift (should be between 0 and 1)
    • Rotation (should be between 0 and 180)
    • Shear (should be between 0 and 1)
    • Zoom (should be between 0 and 1) etc.

Remember, data augmentation should not be used in the validation/test data set.

In [46]:
train_datagen = ImageDataGenerator(
    rotation_range=45, # Slightly increased rotation
    width_shift_range=0.2, # More moderate shift
    height_shift_range=0.2, # More moderate shift
    shear_range=0.2, # More moderate shear
    zoom_range=0.2, # More moderate zoom
    horizontal_flip=True
)

val_datagen = ImageDataGenerator() # No augmentation for validation data

print("ImageDataGenerator for training data (with augmentation) and validation data (without augmentation) have been instantiated.")

ImageDataGenerator for training data (with augmentation) and validation data (without augmentation) have been instantiated.
In [47]:
input_tensor_4 = tf.keras.Input(shape=(200, 200, 3), name='input_image_model4')
x = vgg_model(input_tensor_4, training=False) # Use the pre-trained VGG model with frozen layers
x = Flatten()(x)
x = Dense(128, activation='relu')(x)
x = Dropout(0.2)(x)
x = Dense(64, activation='relu')(x)
output_tensor_4 = Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')(x)

model_4 = tf.keras.Model(inputs=input_tensor_4, outputs=output_tensor_4)

# Compile Model 4
model_4.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

# Display model summary

Model Performance Comparison and Final Model Selection¶

Because of the small amount of data, all of the models achieved a high score on training + validation.

I am going to choose model 4 since it is the most fine tuned model.

Actionable Insights & Recommendations¶

  • So, because the dataset is so small, all of the models were able to memorize the patterns of helmet/no helmet effectively. All of the models are technically overfit.
  • I chose model 4.

Recommendations:

  • More data to train on!!!!! More data would and angles would alow us to tell if the model is actually learning instead of memorizing.
  • Keras has a method called EarlyStopping that will stop training when the model is done improving.
    • Modify the dropout rates for the models (I tried this, did not work very well)

Realistically, VGG16 is too powerful for only 631 images. But this was a good exercise for real implementation

Power Ahead!
